ladder.teaches: the first index where a monotone condition becomes true
ladder.why: The predicate can be derived (nums[i] > nums[0] + i): binary search works whenever something flips exactly once, not only on raw values.
Comparing with the last element splits a rotated array into a false run and a true run, so its minimum is a first-true search.
At every mid one half is sorted; testing whether the target lies in that half decides which half to keep.
Rows that continue one another form one sorted array; index k maps to matrix[k // cols][k % cols].
When only rows and columns are sorted, the top-right corner discards a whole row or column per comparison.
An OA story whose 'continue' is just bisect_right on the sorted breakpoints: the first value strictly greater than x.
Convert times to minutes, then bisect_left finds the first departure at or after now; the >= versus > choice is the whole edge case.
Amazon OA: build a list, sort it once, then answer many 'how many are smaller than x' questions with bisect_left.
Per-key timestamp lists stay sorted for free; each get is the predecessor search bisect_right(ts, t) - 1.
Locating the segment that brackets x is a bisect on the sorted knots, wrapped in interpolation and tie rules.

ladder.teaches: the first index where a monotone condition becomes true
